fetched_contents.text: Oxide growth characteristics, kinetics and mechanism of rutile formation on pure titanium Highlights * • Isothermal oxidation of pure titanium involves two different rate regimes. * • Mathematical model describing the parabolic growth of oxide is developed. * • Marker assisted oxidation of titanium indicates inward growth of oxide. * • Formation of rutile occurs through diffusion of oxygen vacancies. * • Multistage oxidation mechanism for titanium is proposed. Abstract Isothermal oxidation of titanium results in the formation of rutile (TiO2) at temperatures of 600 °C – 1200 °C. Initial growth of TiO2 occurs linearly with an activation energy of 53 kJ/mol. Subsequent growth happens parabolically with an activation energy of 155 kJ/mol determined through a proposed quantitative oxide growth model. Inert particles were located at air/oxide interface, indicating oxygen ions to be dominant component for growth of TiO2. Crystal structure and defect chemistry of TiO2 suggests that oxygen diffuses through TiO2 via oxygen vacancies primarily. Temperature-dependent isothermal oxidation mechanism of titanium is proposed considering experimental results and thermodynamic arguments. Introduction Titanium and its alloys are widely used in several applications such as biological implants, aerospace applications etc. The characteristics of the oxide layer that develops on the surface during oxidation of titanium plays a major role in determining the kind of application the metal can be used for. For e.g., a porous oxide layer is desirable for a good osseointegration during medical implants, whereas an adherent and non-porous oxide layer is desirable for high temperature aerospace applications. There have been several studies on oxidation of titanium at various vacuum conditions. For example, Yetim studied the wear behaviour of titanium oxide films produced by anodic oxidation in different vacuum conditions. The temperature of anodic oxidation in this study varied from −3 to 40 °C. They found the formation of a porous oxide layer on the surface with decreasing pore size with increasing process temperature [1]. Asl et al. compared the wear behaviour of anodically oxidized CP-Ti, Ti–6Al–4V and Ti–45Nb alloys at ambient and vacuum conditions. They reported an increase in hardness of these alloys with oxidation with maximum increase for Ti–45Nb alloy. A more stable wear in vacuum condition than in ambient air was also observed by them [2]. Aniołek studied the thickness, roughness and mechanical properties of thermally grown oxide layers over Grade 2 titanium as a function of oxidation temperature and time [3]. It was reported that the influence of temperature was higher than that of time on the process of oxide layer formation. Out of the two oxidation temperatures they studied, i.e., 600 °C and 700 °C, they reported an isothermal weight gain during 700 °C oxidation to be 5 times higher than 600 °C temperature. Liu et al. explored Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) to assess the morphological characteristics of anodic oxide films formed over titanium [4]. They successfully calculated film thickness and identified oxygen bubbles in the oxide film through high quality images obtained using STEM. Januszewicz et al. studied the effects of glow discharge plasma on oxide layer characteristics during thermal oxidation of Ti6Al4V alloy [5]. They concluded that the presence of grow discharge plasma was disadvantageous due to the formation of complex oxides which were difficult to dissolve. For high temperature applications where the components are made of alloys of titanium, such as in low pressure turbine blades, titanium alloys are susceptible to oxidation in hot air and other gases to which these components get exposed to. Several researchers have studied the oxidation of alloys of titanium in different conditions, for example, air, controlled oxygen, nitrogen, controlled oxygen, and nitrogen environment [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. Exposure of alloys of titanium to these environments results in the formation of varied kinds of stable titanium oxides, Ti3O5, Ti2O3, TiO2 and TiO along with the other predominant elemental oxides [10,11]. Most of the studies have reported the rutile phase, TiO2 to be developed as an oxide layer at high temperatures. Some of the reports also mention about the solubility of oxygen into the titanium at higher temperatures which in turn may adversely affect the mechanical properties of titanium or its alloys [[12], [13], [14], [15]]. The chemical and morphological characteristics of the oxide layer and its growth kinetics govern the overall performance of the functional or structural components made of titanium and hence, it is imperative to study the oxidation mechanism of pure titanium at the temperatures appropriate to applications. Oxidation which involves the growth of one or more oxide phases on any metal is governed by the transport of ions or atoms for the growth of an oxide. In the context of oxidation of pure titanium, very few studies have investigated the diffusion behaviour of titanium and oxygen in the respective Ti–O based phases [16,17], and among these, most of the studies are theoretical [[18], [19], [20]]. Therefore, it is important to establish the mechanism of the formation and growth of the oxide phases on pure titanium with a focus on the diffusion behaviour of different components involved in the oxidation process. fetched_contents.text: Microstructure evolution and oxidation mechanism of TA5 titanium alloy during high-temperature heat treatment Introduction Titanium and titanium alloy are very promising important structural materials owing to their light weight, high specific strength, corrosion resistance, excellent weldability [[1], [2], [3], [4]], and other characteristics. They are currently widely used in aerospace, automotive industry, marine gas turbines, and other industrial fields. The TA5 titanium alloy (Ti–4Al-0.005 B) studied in this paper is an all-α alloy with medium strength, poor plasticity, good weldability, and corrosion resistance. It is usually applied to the stress components, bolts, shafts, and pressure shells of submarines and underwater weapons. The alloy has a close-packed hexagonal (hcp) structure at room temperature and less slip system. Thus, it is easy to form texture during cold rolling, resulting in anisotropy of mechanical properties. In industrial production, cold-rolled titanium plates usually need to undergo high-temperature heat treatment before being placed into actual production applications to achieve the effects of residual stress elimination, dislocation density reduction, uniform microstructure, and improved mechanical properties [[5], [6], [7], [8]]. Moreover, under high-temperature environment, Ti has strong adsorption of O, which can easily enter the surface of titanium alloy substrate. Thus, the oxidation reaction generates a nonprotective brittle O-rich film [9], which considerably affects and limits the mechanical properties of titanium alloy and thus reduces its service life [10]. Therefore, evaluating the oxidation resistance of TA5 titanium alloy at different temperatures and times during high-temperature heat treatment is particularly important. The oxidation of titanium alloy during high-temperature heat treatment refers to the formation of a continuous brittle oxide layer on the surface and the formation of a new oxide at the interface between the oxide layer and the matrix through the diffusion of O2− anion [11]. In Aiying Xi et al.’s work [12], TC18 showed an oxide film composed of Ti3O and TiO2 at 600 °C and 700 °C. The oxide film was composed of three layers of outer Al2O3, secondary outer TiO2, and inner TiO2 at 800 °C. Huiren Jiang et al. [13]. found that the high-temperature oxide of Ti–Al alloy changed with the increase in Al content, forming the outer layer (TiO2) to the inner layer (Al2O3 + TiO2) at a low content, forming the mixed state (Al2O3 + TiO2) at a middle content, and continuously forming Al2O3 at a high content. Since TiO2 exists in a variety of crystal types (rutile, anatase, brookite, etc.). Plate titanium type is a rhombohedral crystal system, which is an unstable crystal type. Rutile is a low-temperature stable phase, and will be transformed into rutile at high temperatures. The rutile crystal structure has a denser atomic arrangement, higher density, hardness, dielectric constant, and greater scattering of light. In the study of Yao et al. [14]. it was found that after oxidation of TA15 titanium alloy at a high temperature of 650–850 °C, the relative content and peak value of TiO2 on the surface were enhanced, and the crystalline type was mainly rutile, and the related crystalline transformation was not observed. In the study of high temperature oxidation of TiCp/Ti64 composites by Huang et al. [15]. it was found that anatase, rutile TiO2 was observed at 500 °C. When the temperature was increased to 600 °C, only rutile TiO2 was observed. Normally, when the temperature is above 600 °C, titanium alloys produce rutile-type TiO2 in the stable state during oxidation. The thickness and composition of the oxide layer formed on the surface at different temperatures and the brittle hardness of the oxide layer can affect the relevant mechanical properties. İlhan Çelik et al. [16]. found that the porous structure of the oxide layer formed on the surface during oxidation may easily lead to crack initiation and deformation, thus reducing strength and plasticity. Similarly, Krzysztof Aniołek et al. [17]. found in their study on Ti–6Al–7Nb that the decrease in mechanical volume properties caused by thermal oxidation may be due to the stress concentration caused by the formation of oxides on the surface, leading to cracks or oxidation grain boundaries under the difference in thermal expansion coefficient. Xiaohui Shi et al. [18]. studied the effect of oxide layer on the fracture toughness of Ti-55511 alloy and found that the presence of oxide layer can reduce the total area of the shear lip and the deflection direction of crack growth of the sample fracture, thus reducing fracture resistance. Many studies have shown that external conditions, alloying, and surface modification can effectively improve high-temperature oxidation resistance to effectively prevent the formation of a large number of brittle oxide layers on the surface. For instance, adding an appropriate amount of Al can form an Al2O3 oxide film protective layer at high temperature, thus preventing further diffusion of O. Meanwhile, V. Optasanu [19] compared the high-temperature oxidation process of various near-α alloys similar to Ti6242 S and found that the higher the N content involved in the reaction, the lower the oxidation degree. This finding indicated that the added alloying element can improve the oxidation resistance by adjusting the N compounds at the interface between oxide and matrix and the concentration of N and O. D.A. Rice et al. [20]. compared the oxidation behavior of TC4 with and without adding B at different temperatures and observed that adding 1 wt% B had the best antioxidant activity. fetched_contents.text: Tribological performance and lubrication mechanism of polyacrylamide as a high-efficiency water-based lubricant additive for titanium alloys Introduction Titanium alloys, particularly TC4, are well-known for their high specific strength, remarkable corrosion resistance, and favorable biocompatibility. These outstanding properties have enabled their extensive application across diverse fields, including aerospace, weaponry and biomedicine1,2. However, titanium alloys exhibit rather poor tribological properties, presenting formidable challenges in the process of lubricating them. These issues not only greatly influence the difficulty and quality of their machining but also impose limitations on their performance within friction pairs3,4,5. The poor tribological properties of titanium alloys result from multiple factors. Their high strength, low modulus, and low thermal conductivity cause problems. High strength leads to significant resistance during friction, while low modulus and thermal conductivity result in poor heat dissipation, making the material prone to severe wear and overheating. Additionally, the tribo-oxide layers on titanium alloys, which are anticipated to afford protection, frequently prove ineffective6. These loose, brittle layers easily fragment. Nonetheless, the role of tribo-oxide layers in the tribological behavior of titanium alloys is a topic of ongoing research. Some studies have presented findings that deviate from the conventional understanding7,8,9,10,11. Philip et al. utilized EDA techniques and found that they could facilitate the formation and existence of deposited layers and tribo-oxides, thereby significantly reducing wear7. Li et al. explored the dry sliding wear behavior of TC4 alloy at sliding velocities ranging from 0.75 to 4 m/s and observed that at a sliding velocity of 4 m/s, the tribo-oxide layer formed rapidly and played a protective role9. Zhang et al. reported that Fe2O3 nanoparticles could accelerate the formation of tribo-oxide layers, effectively reducing the wear rate of the TC4 alloy11. These studies indicate that the formation and stability of tribo-oxide layers are crucial factors that significantly influence the wear behavior and wear resistance of titanium alloys. When it comes to lubrication, conventional liquid lubricants struggle to lubricate titanium alloys due to their unique surface properties, which make it hard to form stable lubrication films4,5. In recent years, water-based lubricants have emerged as a promising alternative because of their economic and environmental benefits, especially their excellent cooling performance12,13,14,15. However, water alone has limited lubrication capabilities. To overcome this limitation, researchers have been actively exploring various lubricant additives, with a focus on environmentally friendly options16,17,18,19,20. For example, Fan et al. investigated tetraalkyl phosphonium perfluorosulfonate ionic liquids and found that they could form a physicochemically adsorbed film on TC4 alloy, enhancing lubrication16. Yang et al. conducted a series of studies on the lubrication of titanium alloys. On the one hand, they found that self-emulsifying ester molecules containing carboxylic acid, ester, and polyethylene glycol (PEG) ester functional groups could adsorb onto the surface of titanium alloys, forming a lubricating film, which effectively mitigated the plowing and abrasive wear on the surface of titanium alloys17. On the other hand, they also studied the lubrication performance of different carbon nanoparticles for titanium alloys and confirmed that these carbon nanoparticles could improve the tribological properties of titanium alloys18. These study findings suggest that the main mechanism by which lubricating additives function is based on the protective film mechanism. The adsorption film mechanism, based on the adsorption of polar functional groups, is a key action mode of lubricating additives. PAM is a widely used water-soluble polymer with a high density of amide groups. This gives it excellent water solubility, biodegradability, chemical reactivity, and adsorption properties. PAM is generally non-toxic to humans and is highly biodegradable in the environment21,22. It also shows good lubricating properties due to its strong adsorption ability, making it valuable in titanium alloy water-based lubrication. For example, Xu synthesized nanoscale PNIPAM microgels and incorporated them into bovine calf serum as a lubricating additive for the contact interface between titanium alloy and ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene23. Results showed that PNIPAM microgels significantly enhanced the lubricity of the bovine calf serum solution. Feng et al. found that poly (N-isopropylacrylamide-co-acrylic acid) microgels, used as water-based lubricating additives, demonstrate excellent lubricating performance for Ti6Al4V friction pairs24. Notably, these microgels lower the friction coefficient by 46% and diminish the wear volume by 45%. Cui et al. constructed a PVA-PAM-PMPC composite structure on the surface of TC4. As a part of the hydrogel coating, PAM is involved in maintaining the stability of the hydrogel coating, ensuring that the interstitial fluid can continuously provide a lubricating effect. This can effectively reduce the friction coefficient, improve the lubrication performance, and reduce wear. Liu accomplished the synthesis of a polyvinyl alcohol/polyacrylamide (PVA/PAAm) hydrogel on the surface of titanium alloy25. Analytical results demonstrate that the resultant hydrogel manifests robust adhesion and remarkable low-friction characteristics. Although certain achievements have been made in the above aspects for PAM, most of the current research focuses on using PAM as a component for constructing microgels or as a modification method for nanomaterials. How temperature affects oxide layer formation on Ti64

Temperature strongly controls the oxidation mechanism, oxide composition, thickness, porosity, and phase stability during oxidation of Ti64 and related titanium alloys. The evidence points to a thermally driven transition from initial oxide growth to a more mature oxide layer as temperature increases.

On the mechanism side, the primary oxidation mechanism appears to involve diffusion-controlled oxide growth, with the oxide layer forming through oxygen vacancies and oxygen ion transport. A direct study on pure titanium reports that isothermal oxidation results in rutile (TiO₂) formation at 600–1200 °C, with initial growth occurring linearly and subsequent growth parabolically [N1-F1]. This indicates a two-stage oxidation mechanism: early linear growth dominated by rapid diffusion processes, and later parabolic growth dominated by slower oxygen diffusion through the oxide layer. Another source states that the oxidation process increases at temperatures higher than 500–600 °C because the oxygen in the atmosphere becomes more active [N1-R2]. This supports a qualitative temperature-dependent activation of oxidation kinetics.

For Ti64-related behavior, the evidence shows that rutile TiO₂ is the stable oxidation product above 600 °C and that anatase and rutile TiO₂ appear at lower temperatures. Huang et al. report that anatase and rutile TiO₂ were observed at 500 °C, and only rutile TiO₂ remained at 600 °C [N2-F2]. A separate review on high-temperature oxidation of TiCp/Ti64 composites similarly notes that rutile TiO₂ is produced at 600 °C and higher, and that the oxide layer may change with temperature [N2-R1]. This suggests that the oxidation mechanism shifts from mixed-phase oxide formation at lower temperatures to rutile-dominated oxidation at higher temperatures.

Oxide thickness, porosity, and composition also change with temperature. The same study on pure titanium reports that oxidation at 600 °C yields a porous oxide layer that is desirable for biomedical implants, while a dense, non-porous layer is preferred for high-temperature aerospace applications [N1-F1]. This is important because porosity can affect both oxidation resistance and mechanical performance. For Ti64, the evidence indicates that higher oxidation temperatures can increase the weight gain and oxide layer thickness more dramatically than time alone. Aniołek’s study on Ti–6Al–4V reports that oxidation at 700 °C gave an isothermal weight gain 5 times higher than at 600 °C [N1-F1]. This implies that oxide thickness increases strongly with temperature, which is consistent with the parabolic-growth behavior of oxide layers in pure titanium [N1-F1].

Porosity is also temperature-sensitive. The evidence states that porous oxide layers can form when temperature is above 700 °C because of volatilization of V₂O₅ [N1-R5]. In addition, the review on TA5 titanium alloy notes that porous structures formed during oxidation may easily lead to crack initiation and deformation, reducing strength and plasticity [N2-F2]. This suggests that as temperature increases, the oxide layer may become more porous and less protective, which can be both advantageous or disadvantageous depending on the application.

Composition changes with temperature as well. The review notes that oxide layers can consist of TiO₂, TiO, Ti₃O₅, Ti₂O₃, and TiO₂, depending on the environment and temperature [N2-F2]. It also reports that at 600 °C and 700 °C, TC18 showed an oxide film composed of Ti₃O and TiO₂, while at 800 °C the oxide film was composed of three layers of outer Al₂O₃, secondary outer TiO₂, and inner TiO₂ [N2-F2]. This shows that higher temperatures can lead to more complex oxide compositions and the formation of protective outer layers such as Al₂O₃. However, the evidence also emphasizes that rutile TiO₂ becomes stable above 600 °C and that the oxide layer may change with temperature [N2-F2].

Phase changes and microstructural evolution are also relevant. The review on TA5 titanium alloy explains that TiO₂ exists in several crystal types, including rutile, anatase, brookite, etc., and that rutile is the low-temperature stable phase, which transforms to rutile at high temperatures [N2-F2]. This suggests a phase transition from lower-temperature oxides to rutile as temperature rises. The same review notes that TiO₂ has a denser atomic arrangement, higher density, hardness, dielectric constant, and greater light scattering [N2-F2], which implies that phase evolution can alter the physical and mechanical properties of the oxide layer.

The evidence also points to microstructural evolution in the alloy itself under oxidation. The review on TA5 titanium alloy states that oxidation during high-temperature heat treatment generates a continuous brittle oxide layer and a new oxide at the interface between oxide layer and matrix through O₂⁻ anion diffusion [N2-F2]. This indicates that oxidation-induced microstructural changes can occur, including the formation of brittle oxide layers and interface oxides. The review also notes that external conditions, alloying, and surface modification can improve oxidation resistance by preventing the formation of brittle oxide layers [N2-F2], which supports the idea that microstructure and oxidation are tightly coupled.

In short, temperature affects oxide formation on Ti64 by shifting the oxidation mechanism from early linear growth to later parabolic growth, increasing oxide thickness and weight gain with higher temperatures, and promoting the formation of rutile-dominated TiO₂ layers at above-600 °C. Porosity can increase with temperature, especially above 700 °C, and composition can become more complex or more protective depending on the environment and temperature. Phase changes such as the formation of rutile and microstructural evolution, including brittle oxide layer formation and interface oxide development, are also important outcomes of oxidation [N1-F1][N2-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
How oxide layers influence Ti64 tribological performance

The evidence indicates that oxide layers on Ti64 can act as both a barrier and a lubricant, depending on their structure, stability, and morphology, and that their role in friction and wear is highly sensitive to these factors. The review on Ti64 tribology emphasizes that the alloy’s poor tribo-behavior is a major limitation, and that surface modification can enhance tribo-performance by improving wear resistance [N5-F4]. It also states that surface modification techniques such as the accretion of adherent appendage layers, diffusion hardening, infusion of residual stresses, microstructural evolution, and phase transformations have been used to improve wear resistance [N5-F4]. This sets the context for oxide layers as one kind of surface modification that can alter tribological behavior.

The direct evidence on oxide layers suggests that they can reduce friction and wear by forming a protective film. The review on Ti64 tribology notes that surface modification can enhance tribo-behavior more effectively than some other methods [N5-F4]. Another source reports that tribological behaviors of titanium alloys lubricated by oil or water-based lubricants are investigated, and that SEE oil phase and aqueous solution showed excellent performance [N3-R3]. This is relevant because oxide layers can function similarly to lubricants by reducing direct metal-to-metal contact.

The most direct evidence on oxide-layer lubrication is the study on polyacrylamide as a water-based lubricant additive. It states that PAM adsorbs on tribo-oxide layers, forming a boundary lubrication film that protects against tribo-oxide loss, reduces friction, and reduces wear [N3-F3]. This is important because it shows that oxide layers themselves can serve as substrates for lubricant films and that these films can protect the oxide layer from degradation. The review also says that the formation and stability of tribo-oxide layers are crucial factors influencing wear behavior and wear resistance [N3-F3]. In other words, a stable oxide layer can support boundary lubrication and reduce wear, while a loose or brittle oxide layer may break away, leading to increased wear.

The evidence also shows that oxide layers can sometimes behave as barriers rather than lubricants. The review notes that high coefficients of friction, intense adhesive wear, and low abrasion resistance are regarded as adverse effects of titanium alloys’ tribological behavior [N3-R2]. In some cases, oxide layers may not reduce wear if they are not stable or if they form in a way that does not support protective lubrication. The review on Ti64 tribology also says that infinite surface modification techniques have been used to enhance wear resistance, implying that some oxide-like surface treatments can be beneficial, but that the alloy’s intrinsic poor tribo-behavior remains a challenge [N5-F4].

The evidence further suggests that the oxide layer can act as an abrasive under certain conditions. The review on TA5 titanium alloy reports that porous oxide layers can easily lead to crack initiation and deformation, reducing strength and plasticity [N2-F2]. This indicates that if the oxide layer becomes brittle or porous, it may not only fail as a protective barrier but may also generate debris or localized stress concentrations that accelerate wear. Similarly, the review on Ti64 tribology emphasizes that surface modification can improve tribo-behavior, but that the alloy’s poor tribological performance remains a major issue [N5-F4]. This supports the idea that oxide-layer stability and morphology are critical determinants of long-term wear resistance.

Layer stability and morphology are especially important for long-term tribological performance. The review on Ti64 tribology states that surface modification techniques such as surface texture, microstructural evolution, and phase transformations can enhance tribo-behavior [N5-F4]. The same review notes that the need is to establish a bridge between indigenous material properties and tribo-characteristics [N5-F4]. This implies that oxide layers, when stable and well-controlled, can help improve tribological performance, but if they become porous, brittle, or unstable, they can degrade performance instead. The review on Ti64 also states that the tribo-behavior of the alloy depends on the surface modification and the interaction with distinct counter-body surfaces [N5-F4], which underscores how oxide-layer morphology and the surrounding environment influence long-term wear.

In summary, oxide layers on Ti64 can modify friction and wear behavior by acting as lubricants, barriers, or abrasives depending on their stability and morphology. A stable, dense, and protective oxide layer can reduce friction and wear, while a porous or brittle oxide layer may accelerate wear by cracking, fragmenting, or generating abrasive debris [N3-F3][N2-F2][N5-F4]. Layer stability and morphology are therefore central to long-term tribological performance [N5-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
How thermal exposure/aging affects oxide behavior and tribology

Thermal exposure and aging can significantly alter oxide-layer stability and tribological performance. The evidence shows that prolonged thermal exposure can increase oxide layer thickness and weight gain, and that higher temperatures can lead to more complex or more brittle oxide compositions. For example, the review on TA5 titanium alloy reports that oxidation during high-temperature heat treatment generates a continuous brittle oxide layer and a new oxide at the oxide/matrix interface [N2-F2]. It also states that the oxide layer may become more brittle with oxidation, reducing strength and plasticity [N2-F2]. This indicates that thermal exposure can change oxide-layer stability in a negative direction.

The evidence also suggests that thermal aging can change oxide-layer stability through microstructural evolution. The same review notes that TiO₂ exists in several crystal types, including rutile, anatase, brookite, etc., and that rutile is the low-temperature stable phase, which transforms to rutile at high temperatures [N2-F2]. It also explains that TiO₂ has a denser atomic arrangement, higher density, hardness, dielectric constant, and greater light scattering [N2-F2]. These properties suggest that phase changes during oxidation can alter the oxide layer’s mechanical and protective behavior. The review further states that external conditions, alloying, and surface modification can improve oxidation resistance by preventing the formation of brittle oxide layers [N2-F2], which implies that thermal aging can either strengthen or weaken oxide-layer stability depending on the environment and alloy composition.

Thermal cycling or oxidation-induced damage can accelerate wear. The review on Ti64 tribology emphasizes that infinite surface modification techniques have been used to improve wear resistance, indicating that some oxide-like surface treatments can enhance tribo-performance, but the alloy’s poor tribological behavior remains a major limitation [N5-F4]. The review also states that the need is to establish a bridge between indigenous material properties and tribo-characteristics, suggesting that repeated thermal exposure may alter the alloy’s microstructure and thereby its wear response [N5-F4]. In addition, the review on TA5 titanium alloy notes that porous oxide layers can easily lead to crack initiation and deformation, reducing strength and plasticity [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that oxidation-induced damage, especially porosity or brittleness, can accelerate wear by creating weak points in the surface.

The evidence also points to thermal aging changing oxide-layer stability through prolonged exposure. The review on TA5 titanium alloy states that oxidation during high-temperature heat treatment generates a continuous brittle oxide layer and that the oxide layer can become brittle with oxidation [N2-F2]. This indicates that prolonged thermal exposure can make oxide layers more brittle, less protective, and more prone to failure. The evidence further notes that the brittle oxide layer can considerably affect and limit the mechanical properties of the alloy, reducing service life [N2-F2]. This is relevant because brittle oxide layers are more likely to fragment or delaminate under mechanical or thermal stress, accelerating wear.

Thermal cycling and oxidation-induced damage can accelerate wear by creating microcracks, porosity, and interface oxides that weaken the surface. The review on TA5 titanium alloy reports that the oxide layer can become porous and brittle, leading to crack initiation and deformation [N2-F2]. It also says that the oxide layer may change with temperature, which suggests that repeated exposure can cause progressive microstructural changes that degrade tribological performance [N2-F2]. The review on Ti64 tribology similarly states that surface modification techniques such as surface texture and microstructural evolution can enhance tribo-behavior, but that the alloy’s poor tribo-behavior remains a major issue [N5-F4]. This implies that thermal aging may reduce the effectiveness of protective oxide layers or other surface treatments over time.

The most relevant tribological metrics under thermal load are wear volume, friction coefficient, hardness, and surface damage indicators. The review on Ti6Al4V tribology notes that the workhorse material’s poor tribo-behavior is reflected in high coefficients of friction, intense adhesive wear, and low abrasion resistance [N3-R2]. It also states that surface modification can enhance tribo-behavior by improving wear resistance [N5-F4]. The study on Ti6Al4V tribology further emphasizes that the tribo-behavior depends on surface modification and the interaction with distinct counter-body surfaces [N5-F4]. This suggests that metrics such as wear volume, friction coefficient, and surface morphology are important for evaluating performance under thermal load. The review on Ti64 tribology also mentions that the need is to understand the microstructural transitions, mechanisms governing tribo-behavior, and parametric conditions leading to material removal at dry sliding conditions [N5-F4]. These are directly relevant metrics for assessing the effects of thermal exposure on tribology.

In conclusion, thermal exposure and aging can change oxide-layer stability by promoting brittleness, porosity, and phase changes, which can either improve or degrade tribological performance depending on the specific conditions. Thermal cycling or oxidation-induced damage can accelerate wear by creating microcracks, interface oxides, and unstable surface layers [N2-F2][N5-F4]. The most relevant tribological metrics under thermal load include wear volume, friction coefficient, hardness, and surface damage indicators [N3-R2][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Evidence for interactions between temperature, oxidation, and tribology

The evidence shows that temperature, oxidation, and tribology are tightly interconnected, with thermal cycling or thermal exposure altering oxide-layer behavior and influencing friction and wear. The studies included here use a variety of experimental conditions and metrics, but the common theme is that temperature drives oxide formation and microstructural evolution, which in turn affects tribological performance.

Thermal cycling or thermal exposure affects oxide-layer behavior by changing oxide composition, thickness, porosity, and phase stability. The review on TA5 titanium alloy reports that oxidation during high-temperature heat treatment generates a continuous brittle oxide layer and a new oxide at the oxide/matrix interface [N2-F2]. It also states that TiO₂ exists in several crystal types, including rutile, anatase, brookite, etc., and that rutile is the low-temperature stable phase, which transforms to rutile at high temperatures [N2-F2]. This indicates that repeated thermal exposure can induce phase changes and alter oxide-layer structure. At the core of oxide formation is a transition from early linear growth to later parabolic growth, with higher temperatures accelerating oxidation kinetics. A direct study on pure titanium reports that isothermal oxidation results in rutile (TiO₂) formation at 600–1200 °C, with initial growth occurring linearly and subsequent growth parabolically [N1-F1]. This means that oxide formation is not uniform across temperature: at lower temperatures, the growth is faster, while at higher temperatures, the growth slows relative to time, reflecting diffusion-controlled oxide thickening [N1-F1]. ## Integrated explanation of how temperature affects oxide layer formation and how those layers influence Ti64 tribological performance

Temperature has a profound effect on oxide layer formation on Ti64 and related titanium alloys. The evidence points to a thermally driven oxidation mechanism in which oxide thickness, porosity, composition, and phase stability evolve with temperature, and in which oxidation can either improve or worsen tribological performance depending on the resulting oxide-layer state.

### 1) How temperature affects oxide layer formation on Ti64

At the core of oxide formation is a transition from early linear growth to later parabolic growth, with higher temperatures accelerating oxidation kinetics. A direct study on pure titanium reports that isothermal oxidation results in rutile (TiO₂) formation at 600–1200 °C, with initial growth occurring linearly and subsequent growth parabolically [N1-F1]. This means that oxide formation is not uniform across temperature: at lower temperatures, the growth is faster, while at higher temperatures, the growth slows relative to time, reflecting diffusion-controlled oxide thickening [N1-F1]. Another source states that oxidation becomes more active at temperatures above 500–600 °C, which aligns with the general temperature dependence of oxidation and suggests that the threshold for significant oxide growth is not abrupt but rather gradual [N1-R2].

For Ti64-related behavior, the evidence shows that rutile TiO₂ becomes the dominant oxide phase above 600 °C and that lower-temperature oxidation can produce mixed oxide phases. Huang et al. report that anatase and rutile TiO₂ were observed at 500 °C, and only rutile TiO₂ remained at 600 °C [N2-F2]. A separate review on high-temperature oxidation of TiCp/Ti64 composites similarly notes that rutile TiO₂ is produced at 600 °C and higher and that the oxide layer may change with temperature [N2-R1]. This indicates a clear temperature-dependent shift in oxide composition and phase, with rutile becoming stable and dominant above 600 °C.

Oxide thickness, porosity, and composition also change with temperature. The same study on pure titanium says that oxidation at 600 °C yields a porous oxide layer, while a dense, non-porous layer is preferred for high-temperature aerospace applications [N1-F1]. This is important because porosity affects both oxidation resistance and mechanical performance. For Ti64, higher oxidation temperatures can increase the weight gain and oxide layer thickness more dramatically than time alone. Aniołek’s study on Ti–6Al–4V reports that oxidation at 700 °C gave an isothermal weight gain 5 times higher than at 600 °C [N1-F1]. This suggests that oxide thickness increases strongly with temperature, which is consistent with the parabolic-growth behavior of oxide layers [N1-F1].

Porosity becomes more significant at higher temperatures. The evidence states that porous oxide layers can form when temperature is above 700 °C because of volatilization of V₂O₅ [N1-R5]. The review on TA5 titanium alloy notes that porous structures formed during oxidation may easily lead to crack initiation and deformation, reducing strength and plasticity [N2-F2]. This implies that as temperature rises, the oxide layer can become more porous and less protective, which can be beneficial for biomedical implants but disadvantageous for high-temperature applications [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Composition also changes with temperature. The review notes that oxide layers can consist of TiO₂, TiO, Ti₃O₅, Ti₂O₃, and TiO₂, depending on the environment and temperature [N2-F2]. It also reports that at 600 °C and 700 °C, TC18 showed an oxide film composed of Ti₃O and TiO₂, while at 800 °C the oxide film was composed of three layers of outer Al₂O₃, secondary outer TiO₂, and inner TiO₂ [N2-F2]. This shows that higher temperatures can lead to more complex oxide compositions and the formation of protective outer layers such as Al₂O₃. However, the evidence also emphasizes that rutile TiO₂ becomes stable above 600 °C and that the oxide layer may change with temperature [N2-F2].

Phase changes and microstructural evolution are also important. The review on TA5 titanium alloy explains that TiO₂ exists in several crystal types, including rutile, anatase, brookite, etc., and that rutile is the low-temperature stable phase, which transforms to rutile at high temperatures [N2-F2]. This suggests a phase transition from lower-temperature oxides to rutile as temperature rises. The review also notes that TiO₂ has a denser atomic arrangement, higher density, hardness, dielectric constant, and greater light scattering [N2-F2], which implies that phase evolution can alter the physical and mechanical properties of the oxide layer.

Porosity can increase with temperature, especially above 700 °C, and composition can become more complex or more protective depending on the environment and temperature. Phase changes such as the formation of rutile and microstructural evolution, including brittle oxide layer formation and interface oxide development, are also important outcomes of oxidation [N1-F1][N2-F2].

It also says that surface modification techniques such as the accretion of adherent appendage layers, diffusion hardening, infusion of residual stresses, microstructural evolution, and phase transformations have been used to improve wear resistance [N5-F4]. This sets the context for oxide layers as one kind of surface modification that can alter tribological behavior.

The most direct evidence on oxide-layer lubrication comes from the study on polyacrylamide as a water-based lubricant additive. It states that PAM adsorbs on tribo-oxide layers, forming a boundary lubrication film that protects against tribo-oxide loss, reduces friction, and reduces wear [N3-F3]. The review on Ti64 tribology also notes that the formation and stability of tribo-oxide layers are crucial factors influencing wear behavior and wear resistance [N3-F3].
